title: Why Collections Are Needed
learningObjectives: Explain why programs use collections to store groups of related values.
Compare storing repeated items in separate variables with storing them in one collection.
Describe how collections support iteration, searching, grouping, and updates.
Identify a collection's order, access method, and data constraints.
Choose a collection approach based on the task instead of convenience alone.

understand.concept: A collection stores multiple values under one organized structure. Instead of creating separate variables for every item, a program can group related values and work with them through operations such as adding, reading, searching, counting, sorting, or removing. Collections make repeated data manageable as the amount of information grows.
understand.whyItMatters: Most programs work with groups of data: products, messages, scores, users, sensor readings, or tasks. Collections reduce repetitive code and enable scalable processing, but choosing the right collection affects access, uniqueness, ordering, and performance.
understand.analogy: A collection is like a tray with compartments for related items. You can count the items, inspect one, add another, or remove one without inventing a new tray for every item.
understand.analogyLimit: Different collection types organize items differently. A tray analogy does not explain key-based lookup, uniqueness, memory growth, or all performance trade-offs.

explain.narrative: When the program has several values that share a role, a collection provides one name for the group. The program can use a loop to process all items and collection operations to manage the group. Collections may preserve order, enforce uniqueness, use indexes, or use keys. Ask how the task needs to retrieve items and whether duplicate values are meaningful before choosing a type.

examples.title: Separate variables become repetitive
examples.code: let item1 = 'pen'; let item2 = 'book'; let item3 = 'bag';
examples.explanation: Each item needs a separate name, which becomes awkward when the number of items changes.

examples.title: Group related values
examples.explanation: One collection represents the group, so a loop can process all values.

examples.title: Count items
examples.explanation: A collection provides a way to obtain the group size without counting individual variables manually.

examples.title: Process each item
examples.explanation: Iteration applies one operation to every element in the group.

examples.title: Add an item
examples.explanation: A collection can be extended with a supported operation instead of creating another standalone variable.

commonMistakes: Using unrelated values in one collection without a clear meaning.
Assuming every collection preserves order or permits duplicates.
Hard-coding item-specific variables when the number of items can grow.
Choosing a collection without considering lookup and update needs.
Confusing the collection with a single item stored inside it.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Plan a collection operation
guidedTask.instructions: Use "Why Collections Are Needed" to solve a small data-management task.
steps: Describe the group of data and whether order matters.
Choose the collection type and explain why.
Show an operation that reads or changes the collection.
Trace what happens to size or positions.
Test empty, single-item, and typical cases as appropriate.
guidedTask.starterCode: const collection = []; // plan your collection example

independentTask.title: Independent: Manage a changing data group
independentTask.instructions: Build a small collection scenario using your own values and demonstrate the operations.
requirements: Show the resulting size or item positions.
Explain why this collection type fits.

hints: Ask whether order, indexes, uniqueness, or keys matter.
Use the length/size value instead of hard-coding counts.
Insertion and removal can change later positions.
Test an empty collection and one item before larger cases.
